strengths: Jointly optimizing pipeline placement and per-layer DP, TP, and FSDP addresses a useful training-infrastructure problem. Evaluation on ViT-Huge and Swin-Huge establishes relevance to computer vision.

The measured improvements are meaningful: Table 2 reports 1.10–1.70× throughput gains over Galvatron, while Table 1 reports 6.36–16.83× search-time reductions. UniAP also trains Swin-Huge in an environment where Galvatron encounters OOM. Faster search remains valuable when training throughput matches the baseline.

Table 3 demonstrates benefits of combining parallelism types for BERT and T5. Appendix D provides an informative example combining pipeline parallelism across nodes with TP, DP, and selective FSDP within nodes.
The overview, optimization pseudocode, hardware specifications, and appendix descriptions of model configurations and solver settings provide useful methodological transparency.
weaknesses: The central formulation has a consequential communication-accounting gap. Contiguity constraints do not enforce the ordering of pipeline stages, while Eq. (3) counts only edges from stage j to j+1. For a two-layer chain u→v, assigning u to stage 2 and v to stage 1 satisfies the stated placement and contiguity constraints but incurs zero modeled cross-stage communication. Edges spanning nonadjacent stages are also unaccounted for. These omissions can change the optimizer's preferred solution; the manuscript does not establish how the implementation avoids them.

The displayed optimization is not quadratic as written. Eqs. (2) and (3) multiply two placement variables by a bilinear strategy-selection term, producing fourth-degree products. Auxiliary variables could enable a reformulation, but the required variables and constraints are not supplied. This leaves a substantial gap between the advertised MIQP and the problem actually passed to Gurobi.

The global-optimality guarantee is unsupported by the reported solver procedure. Appendix C specifies a 60-second time limit and permits termination after 15 seconds with a relative optimality gap below 4%, without reporting achieved gaps. Section 3.6 then treats the solver timeout as constant to claim O(|V||g|log n) complexity. A timeout bounds a truncated procedure; it does not establish that globally optimal solutions can be obtained with that complexity.

The cost model is insufficiently validated for the strength of the optimality claims. Eq. (1) relies on aligned forward/backward bottlenecks and computation dominating communication, while Section 3.3 assumes computation time scales linearly with batch size. No predicted-versus-measured timing or strategy-ranking validation is provided. Consequently, even an exact optimization would establish optimality only for an approximate model within the restricted search space.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of unified optimization. Galvatron is the only measured baseline, although the related-work discussion identifies Alpa and Piper as supporting hybrid parallelism. Table 3 removes entire parallelism categories rather than comparing unified and hierarchical optimization over matched candidates and costs. It therefore supports hybrid parallelism's usefulness without establishing the claimed advantage of the particular joint formulation over hierarchical approaches.

Efficiency and reproducibility evidence remain incomplete. Reported search times exclude profiling, and the strategy dictionary and cost-construction routines lack sufficient detail for faithful reconstruction. Figure 4 changes batch size with node count over only 1–4 nodes, supporting limited weak-scaling evidence rather than validating the asymptotic analysis. These limitations reinforce the reservations, but the unresolved formulation correctness and unsupported guarantees are the principal reasons the balance favors weak rejection.
